safe.facts: University of Washington × UW Medicine · Sept–Dec 2023 · product designer · 3 designers, 1 PM
safe.note: Content note: this project discusses sexual assault.
safe.q: How might we create a safe space for sexual assault survivors during preventative healthcare appointments?
safe.problem: Gynecologist visits often feel cold and transactional. For survivors of sexual trauma, routine invasive exams like pelvic exams or pap smears can be retriggering, even retraumatizing.

quote.t: One of the hallmarks of trauma experiences is loss of control.

research.t: We read survivor and nurse communities online, booked an appointment to observe the exam room, surveyed survivors, providers and educators, then ran six interviews. I led two of them.

steps.d: Patients see the exams they’re due for and pre-select them, can choose to disclose a history of trauma and ask for accommodations, and see their rights clearly before signing consent.

A clinic tablet lets patients set the temperature and lighting and choose calming ceiling projections. Chairs sit below the patient’s line of sight, and a comfort box holds stress balls and warming pads.
A short post-visit questionnaire lets patients reflect on the visit and shape their future care.

safe.learned: Even small changes, like a few extra steps when booking, can change how safe care feels.

closing.cap: Team FourGood, beaming after the final presentation.

hpe.facts: Hewlett Packard Enterprise · Advanced Development Centre · Sept 2022–Mar 2023 · UX designer, with a senior UX designer, an engineer and a PM
hpe.note: Details are under NDA. She’s happy to talk about it.
hpe.problem: AI models get less accurate as they see new data. It’s called data drift. Data scientists were checking too many different tools to catch it in time.

quote.t: By the time we notice a significant performance drop, it’s often too late.

steps.d: Interviewed data scientists and ML engineers, then shadowed their day to feel the pain first-hand.
A single dashboard for model performance and data distributions in real time, with early warnings and automated retraining.
Built in React and Grommet with our developer, on HPE’s design system, and tested on live production data.

hpe.learned: Complex data mustn’t be dumbed down for usability. This was her first design job after software engineering, and the project where she decided to become a designer.

github.facts: GitHub × University of Washington · Jan–Mar 2024 · product designer & researcher · 3 designers, 1 senior researcher, 1 PM
github.q: How might we improve code review for better collaboration among developers?
github.problem: In early 2024 GitHub was beta-testing a more “accessible” code review with floating comments. In usability tests it scored lower than the design it was replacing.

research.t: We tested with six experienced developers across four setups (old and new UI, as code author and as reviewer), varying the order to avoid bias.

steps.d: Four of six developers used multiple monitors, so right-aligned comments meant constant scanning. We moved the indicators left and made the whole line clickable: 60% less mouse movement, 25% faster reviews.
Long discussions broke flow when floating. A setting now switches between floating and inline comments.
Colour-blind developers struggled to spot the new comment indicators on highlighted code, so we raised the contrast.
Comment counts in the file tree, so no one hunts for discussions: 40% faster file navigation.

github.learned: “Accessible” isn’t always accessible. It means understanding how people actually work, not just following guidelines. The study shaped GitHub’s roadmap for the feature.

closing.cap: How a few seconds saved per comment ripple out across GitHub.
